configs.what: Auto mode, the built-in starting mode for interactive terminal and VS Code sessions from v2.1.283 (on earlier versions only on Pro, Max, Ultra and Team plans): a classifier reviews actions instead of the person. claude -p and the Agent SDK start in Manual mode; auto mode needs a supported model, and an organisation can turn it off.
Shell commands confined by the operating system.
The person chooses Manual mode: shell commands and edits ask first.
Managed settings, permission rules and telemetry.
Everything that widens what it does.

facts.label: It works across several domains or systems
facts.fact: The repository, the shell and the code host.

facts.label: Several agents coordinate inside the organisation
facts.fact: The cloud page says agent teams are off by default and are enabled with an environment variable; the agent teams page describes instances, each in its own context, that message each other.
facts.quote: Agent teams are off by default but can be enabled

facts.label: The agent works independently; the person approves critical decisions only
facts.fact: In Accept edits, which the permission modes page says corresponds to the default mode in cloud sessions, Claude makes changes and pushes a branch without stopping for approval; the person reviews the result The permission modes page adds that Accept edits corresponds to the default mode in cloud sessions.
facts.quote: Claude makes changes and pushes a branch without stopping for approval

facts.label: It connects to external tools or services across a trust boundary
facts.fact: Sessions reach package registries and other allowlisted domains.

facts.label: The data it uses is described
facts.fact: A page describes what data is sent, kept and used.

facts.label: The models and third-party components it uses are listed
facts.fact: The model configuration page lists the models Claude Code uses by alias and the version each resolves to per provider; cloud sessions take the same /model command.
facts.quote: Uses the latest Opus model for complex reasoning tasks

facts.label: It works across several domains or systems
facts.fact: The codebase, the shell, git and the development tools it integrates with.

facts.label: Several agents coordinate inside the organisation
facts.fact: Agent teams coordinate several instances, each in its own context, that message each other. The vendor says they "are experimental and disabled by default".

facts.label: The agent works independently; the person approves critical decisions only
facts.fact: From v2.1.283, auto mode is the built-in starting mode for terminal and VS Code sessions: a classifier reviews actions instead of prompting; an action it blocks is listed, and the person can approve it so Claude may retry.
facts.quote: approve the action so Claude may retry

facts.label: It connects to external tools or services across a trust boundary
facts.fact: It can connect to Model Context Protocol servers; a project’s servers have their own approval prompt.

facts.label: A limit on it is enforced by something outside its own reach
facts.fact: Sandboxing restricts shell commands at the operating system level (filesystem and network) on macOS, Linux and WSL2; on native Windows, commands run unsandboxed. The page says it is off by default, that it covers shell commands only while the file tools, MCP servers and hooks run outside it, and that Claude can ask to run a command unsandboxed unless strict sandbox mode is on.
facts.quote: The sandbox is off by default

facts.label: Policy is enforced as machine-readable rules
facts.fact: An organisation can deliver managed settings, and nothing in a user's own settings files or the --settings flag overrides a managed key. This is an enforcement mechanism, not a policy. It applies only where an organisation deploys managed settings.

facts.label: Its limits and known failure cases are documented for those who use it
facts.fact: The security page states limits, for example that an approved shell command can write anywhere the account can.

facts.label: The data it uses is described
facts.fact: A page describes what data is sent, kept and used.

help.label: Our hypothesis, not their claim. Built from public pages only; nothing of theirs was tested.
help.pitch: RiskMandate would measure, for one real deployment of Anthropic's agents, what each agent was asked to do (its mandate), what its credentials and connections actually let it reach (its grant), and the difference between the two (the gap), and keep that as a written record. It is read-only: never in the request path.
